content: In chemistry and physics, matter is typically defined as the substance that constitutes physical objects, excluding the contributions of various energy or force fields, which are not generally considered matter in the strict sense, even though they may contribute to the mass of objects. Matter makes up much of the observable universe, although light is not usually classified as matter. However, the term matter is somewhat loosely defined for scientific purposes. Matter is composed of chemical substances, which are made up of atoms. Atoms themselves consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons. In this context, matter is often contrasted with energy, although energy can be considered an expression of matter. In physics, there is no universally agreed-upon definition of matter. Physicists often avoid using the term when precision is required, instead referring to more clearly defined concepts such as mass, energy, and particles. Some physicists define matter as anything composed of elementary fermions, which include leptons (such as electrons) and quarks (such as up and down quarks, which make up protons and neutrons). Since protons, neutrons, and electrons combine to form atoms, and atoms combine to form molecules and bulk substances, all of these are considered matter. Matter also includes baryons and mesons. However, things like light (photons) and other gauge bosons are not considered matter. This definition of matter is not always entirely satisfactory. For example, some entities may have mass without being classified as matter: W and Z bosons have mass but are not elementary fermions. A system of two photons not moving parallel to each other has an invariant mass. Glueballs have mass due to their binding energy but contain no particles with mass or elementary fermions. Conversely, some entities may be considered matter without having mass: Most of the mass of protons and neutrons arises from the binding energy between quarks, not the quarks' intrinsic masses. One type of neutrino may be massless. The up quark may also be massless. There is a semantic difficulty with the term matter because it has two meanings, one of which includes the other. For example, both electrons and positrons are considered matter in one sense but not in another. A similar issue arises with the term particle. Quarks combine to form hadrons, such as protons and neutrons. Due to the principle of color confinement in the strong interaction, quarks never exist unbound from other quarks. Protons and neutrons typically form atomic nuclei, which are surrounded by a cloud of electrons. A nucleus with an equal number of protons and electrons is electrically neutral and is called an atom; otherwise, it is an ion. Leptons, such as electrons, do not experience the strong force and can exist unbound from other particles. On Earth, electrons are usually bound in atoms, but they can be easily freed, as seen in cathode ray tubes. Muons can briefly form bound states known as muonic atoms. Neutrinos, which do not interact via the strong or electromagnetic forces, are never bound to other particles. Homogeneous matter has a uniform composition and properties, regardless of the amount. It can be a mixture, like brass, or elemental, like pure iron. Heterogeneous matter, such as granite, does not have a uniform composition. In bulk, matter can exist in various phases depending on pressure and temperature. These phases include solids, liquids, gases, plasmas, superfluids, supersolids, Bose-Einstein condensates, fermionic condensates, liquid crystals, strange matter, and quark-gluon plasmas. Magnetic materials can also exhibit paramagnetic and ferromagnetic phases. Changes in conditions can cause matter to transition between phases, a process studied in thermodynamics. In small quantities, matter can exhibit properties distinct from bulk material and may not fit neatly into any phase. Phases are sometimes referred to as states of matter, but this can cause confusion with thermodynamic states. For example, two gases at different pressures are in different thermodynamic states but the same state of matter. Antimatter, in particle physics and quantum chemistry, is composed of antiparticles corresponding to the particles of normal matter. When a particle and its antiparticle come into contact, they annihilate, converting into other particles with equivalent energy, as described by Einstein's equation (E = mc^2). These new particles may include high-energy photons (gamma rays) or other particle-antiparticle pairs. The resulting particles carry kinetic energy equal to the difference between the rest mass of the annihilation products and the original particle-antiparticle pair. Antimatter is not naturally found on Earth, except in extremely small quantities produced by radioactive decay or cosmic rays. This is because any antimatter that forms on Earth would almost immediately encounter ordinary matter and annihilate. Antiparticles and stable antimatter, such as antihydrogen, can be created in laboratories in tiny amounts, but not in sufficient quantities for practical applications. The apparent asymmetry between matter and antimatter in the observable universe is one of the major unsolved problems in physics. Possible explanations for this asymmetry are explored under the concept of baryogenesis. In cosmology, most models of the early universe and the Big Bang require the existence of dark matter. Dark matter has energy and mass but is not composed of elementary fermions or gauge bosons. Instead, it is thought to consist of particles unknown to current science. Its existence is inferred rather than directly observed.
